paras: The lynching of an alleged cattle thief near Coleman, Texas, was the hanging in late November 1882 of an unnamed man described as one of a gang charged with stealing cattle near Comanche. It was one of several hangings of the alleged gang's members within about a week, which Texas and wire reports said broke the gang up. No report gives the man's name, his race, or who hanged him.

According to a Dallas dispatch, a gang of "desperadoes" had been stealing cattle and "committing other depredations" in the neighborhood of Comanche for some time. A special correspondent at Comanche wrote that four men were charged with the theft, which he described as stealing cattle from "a poor widow."

One of the four was "captured and hung near Coleman last week," the Comanche correspondent reported on December 1, without giving a day, a place more exact than "near Coleman," or any account of the men who did it. A second man was then caught and hanged at a place in Comanche County printed variously as Siepe Springs, Deep Springs and Liege Springs. Two more, named Terry, were taken from officers by a mob at Hazel Dell and hanged from a tree, on a Friday night by the wire's account.

The Herald's correspondent said the hangings "cleaned them all up," and the Dallas wire said it was believed the gang had been broken up. No report of an inquest, arrest or prosecution for the Coleman hanging appears in the coverage.

The Dallas Daily Herald printed the news on December 2 in a column of specials, placing the hangings between an account of a Thanksgiving Day fire at Comanche and the line "Business is good." A Dallas telegram dated December 3 carried the story north and east under the headline "A Gang of Desperadoes," calling the hanged men "outlaws"; the Wheeling Register ran it on December 4. Weekly news digests in Minnesota and Dakota repeated it on December 6 and 7, saying the gang had been "summarily dealt with by the injured Texasans" and using the word "lynched" for the Coleman hanging.

Every version treated the killing in a single sentence as part of a gang's breakup, and none questioned it or named the man. No Black-press coverage was found, and no local Coleman account appears in the coverage.

chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: An unnamed man accused as one of a cattle-stealing gang was 'caught and hung near Coleman' outside any legal process, which a digest called being 'lynched' (A1, A2, A7).

The man was hanged after capture on an accusation of cattle stealing with no court involved, and a digest calls it a lynching (A1, A2, A7); no report says who did it or how many took part, so the group-of-three element rests on the word 'lynched' alone.
Every report is a one-sentence mention that traces to Dallas reporting from Comanche (A1's special and the Dallas wire, A2), so there is no independent local account of the Coleman hanging itself.
